To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) normal B lymphocytes can produce autoantibodies against thyroglobulin and thyroid microsomal antigens in vitro in the absence of antigenic stimulation, 2) the induction of autoantibodies by normal CD4 helper/inducer cells is enhanced by the addition of thyroid microsomal or thyroglobulin antigen, 3) CD4 cells from Graves' disease patients have enhanced helper activity for autoantibody induction by thyroid microsomal but not

1) normal autologous or alloge-neic CD4 cells are capable of helping the induction of AMA-secreting cells from normal B lymphocytes in the presence of thyroid microsomal antigens; 2) CD4 cells from AITD patients are more efficient than normal cells in helping the induction of anti-McAg-secreting cells; and 3), normal CD8 cells suppress the induction of AMA secreting cells by PWM more efficiently than do CD8 cells
the helper activity of normal CD4 (helper-inducer) cells to induce anti-thyroid autoantibody-secreting cells is relatively impaired in patients with autoimmune thyroid diseases.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the immunoregulation of the induction and suppression of anti-thyroglobulin and anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody-secreting B cells by CD4 (helper) and CD8 (supressor/cytotoxic) lymphocyte subpopulations.
the immunoregulation of thyroid autoimmunity.
the induction of autoantibody-secreting cells from normal subjects by autologous CD8 cells and autologus or allogeneous CD4 cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the induction of anti-thyrodi microsomal antibody secreting cells from normal subjects is a complex process, involving a number of immunological factors.

the immune system is capable of producing autoimmunity in the absence of disease and that disease is the result of a breakdown of self-tolerance, a process which may be the result of genetic or environmental factors or both.

the induction of anti-thyroperoxidase antibody-secreting B cells in vitro by autologous CD8+ T cells in normal subjects is suppressed by CD4+ T cells, whereas in patients with Graves' disease, this suppressive activity is impaired.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the helper function of T cells in the induction and secretion of autoantibodies by B cells is not impaired in AITD, and that the impaired suppressor function of T cells is responsible for the breakdown in self-tolerance in AITD.
we have demonstrated that the induction of autoantibodies to thyroid microsomes can be induced in vitro in B lymphocytes from normals by the combination of CD4 and CD8 cells.

the helper activity of autologous or heterologous CD4 lymphocytes from patients with AID is greater than that from normal subjects, and this helper activity is due, at least in part, to the relatively impaired suppressor function of thyroid antigen-specific CD4 lymphocytes in patients with AITDs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CD8 cells play an important role to maintain self-tolerance.
the helper activity of T cells from patients with autoimmune thyroid diseases is greater than that in healthy individuals.
the immune system is not a simple system.
